candidates.attacker_control: A remote, unauthenticated peer fully controls the raw HTTP/1.x header bytes parsed by Netty: request headers in server/proxy deployments and response headers in client deployments. Supplying a Content-Length header together with Transfer-Encoding: chunked (or duplicate/invalid Content-Length fields) is sufficient to reach the framing decision in HttpObjectDecoder.readHeaders; no credentials or local access are needed.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The CVE-2019-16869 whitespace-before-colon variant appears mitigated in this snapshot: header-name validation in DefaultHttpHeaders rejects space/tab/control characters (validateHeaderNameElement, lines 362-409), so not every smuggling variant works. HttpUtil.setTransferEncodingChunked(m, true) does remove Content-Length (315-318), but the decode path never invokes it for the TE+CL case; it is only used when constructing outbound messages. Duplicate Content-Length values that are comma-joined in one field cause Long.parseLong to throw and the message to be invalidated, so that specific variant is rejected. Applications that rebuild headers before forwarding can neutralize the issue. No runtime testing or upstream fix/history comparison was possible in this run.
candidates.impact: HTTP request/response smuggling and connection desynchronization. A remote attacker can make a front-end and back-end (or application logic) disagree about message boundaries, which classically enables security-control bypass, cache poisoning, request/credential capture, and poisoning of subsequent requests on shared connections. Secondary impact: Netty messages/aggregated messages can carry a Content-Length that contradicts the actual content, so applications reasoning from the header may mis-process data.
candidates.prerequisites: A deployment where Netty's HTTP codec (HttpServerCodec/HttpClientCodec/HttpObjectAggregator or an application built on it) shares a persistent connection with another HTTP interpreter (reverse proxy, load balancer, CDN, or back-end/application logic) and the messages are forwarded or their framing headers are trusted. The two components must disagree on whether Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding determines the body boundary. Applications that fully re-normalize/rewrite framing headers before use are not affected.
candidates.root_cause: HttpObjectDecoder.readHeaders decides body framing by checking HttpUtil.isTransferEncodingChunked(message) first and, when true, moves to READ_CHUNK_SIZE without rejecting, removing, or otherwise normalizing a coexisting Content-Length header; the parsed Content-Length remains attached to the message (lines 573-598, 605-614). The non-chunked path derives length via HttpUtil.getContentLength, which reads only the first Content-Length value through headers().get(...) and parses it with Long.parseLong without validating duplicate/conflicting or malformed values (HttpUtil.java 174-189), and isTransferEncodingChunked only matches an exact 'chunked' value (HttpUtil.java 303-305). No compensating normalization exists in the outbound path either: HttpObjectEncoder frames by the TE header and its sanitizeHeadersBeforeEncode is a no-op (lines 90-101, 226-231), HttpRequestEncoder adds no sanitization (28-79), and HttpObjectAggregator removes only the TE header while retaining the attacker's Content-Length (204-242). Thus decoded and re-encoded messages carry contradictory framing metadata.
candidates.title: HTTP/1 decoder accepts both Transfer-Encoding: chunked and Content-Length without normalization, enabling request smuggling
candidates.trace: Inbound bytes -> HttpObjectDecoder.decode READ_HEADER state (line 214) -> readHeaders parses all header fields into the message (lines 573-598, adding both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length) -> line 608 isTransferEncodingChunked(message) is true, so nextState = READ_CHUNK_SIZE (609) and the attacker's Content-Length is left in the headers; the contentLength()/HttpUtil.getContentLength path (618-623, 174-189) is only used for the non-chunked branch and returns the first Content-Length value if the application asks -> the decoded HttpMessage (out.add(message), line 232) therefore advertises a Content-Length while the connection was actually framed as chunked, and the bytes after the chunk terminator are parsed as the next message on the same connection. If the message is forwarded, HttpObjectEncoder frames by Transfer-Encoding (line 97) and re-emits the Content-Length because sanitizeHeadersBeforeEncode is a no-op (229-231) and HttpRequestEncoder adds no sanitization; HttpObjectAggregator likewise keeps the attacker's Content-Length after aggregation (237-241). A peer that trusts Content-Length then consumes the following request bytes as body, desynchronizing the two interpreters.
candidates.unverified: Exploitability is not runtime-confirmed: it depends on a second HTTP interpreter in the deployment that prefers Content-Length while Netty prefers Transfer-Encoding (or vice versa), and on messages/connections being reused or forwarded. I also could not diff this snapshot against the upstream fix commit, so the mapping to a specific CVE/advisory is inferred from the missing normalization logic and the project's later addition of Content-Length normalization/duplicate handling, not verified against repository history.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request Smuggling') (related CWE-436)

coverage_summary: Scope reported by get_source_scope: 1,851 model-visible source files, 0 excluded by size/symlink/sensitive-name filters, binary-like files skipped on NUL detection; the snapshot contains only main sources (no src/test trees). I read the HTTP/1 codec deeply (HttpObjectDecoder, HttpUtil, HttpObjectEncoder, HttpRequestEncoder/HttpResponseEncoder, HttpObjectAggregator, DefaultHttpHeaders, HttpPost*RequestDecoder spot checks), examined HTTP/2 framing/HPACK entry points, the NIO/IoHandler transport code, DNS codec decompression, MQTT decoder bounds, XML decoder factory setup, and the root/all poms and Docker CI files for version/timeline context. No precomputed relation index or history was available, so coverage is search/read based rather than exhaustive; large modules such as full SSL/TLS handler, native transports, and multipart encoders were only spot-checked.
limitations: No runtime execution, network interaction, or exploit validation was performed; the finding is a source-level lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
No git history, commit metadata, tests, or upstream fix diff is present in the snapshot, so the mapping to a specific advisory/CVE and to the exact vulnerable revision is inferred, not verified.
Attacker impact depends on deployment topology (presence of a second HTTP interpreter and message forwarding); this cannot be determined from the repository alone.
Only main sources are present (no tests), which removes behavioral examples that could confirm intended framing semantics.
The broad repository sweep was search-driven; files without security-relevant keywords or in modules not examined in depth may contain other issues.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded decompression/allocation in zlib/gzip (JdkZlibDecoder/JZlibDecoder) and Bzip2 decoders (CVE-2020-11612, CVE-2021-37136/37137 family).
rejected_leads.reason: No max-allocation/decompression-ratio guard is visible in these decoders, but this snapshot is Netty 5.0.0.Final-SNAPSHOT with 2019-era dependencies (netty-tcnative 2.0.28, GraalVM 19.0.0, Conscrypt 1.3.0), so those 2020/2021 fixes are far later than the snapshot's timeline; the issue is real but not the strongest/timely candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: HttpPostRequestDecoder/multipart issues: insecure temp-file handling (CVE-2021-21290) and unbounded memory buffering (CVE-2024-29025).
rejected_leads.reason: Same timeline mismatch (fixes 2021/2024) and the temp-file issue is local-only; no clear attacker-controlled path to a stronger impact was established from source.

rejected_leads.lead: SniHandler/AbstractSniHandler unbounded ClientHello accumulation (CVE-2023-34462, no maxClientHelloLength in this snapshot).
rejected_leads.reason: Later fix timeline; requires TLS deployment specifics and is a memory-exhaustion issue rather than a framing/trust-boundary bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: XmlDecoder uses Aalto InputFactoryImpl without disabling DTD/external entities (possible XXE).
rejected_leads.reason: Could not establish from source that external entities/DTD are enabled by default for this parser, and no repository evidence (config, tests, comments) ties it to a fix; unconfirmed.
Appears already mitigated: HttpObjectDecoder delegates request header-name validation to DefaultHttpHeaders, whose validator rejects space/tab/control characters; no unfixed path found.

rejected_leads.lead: HttpUtil.getContentLength accepting unusual numeric forms (leading '+', leading zeros, negative values) as a standalone issue.
rejected_leads.reason: Real normalization gap but part of the same root cause (framing-header normalization) as the selected candidate; not split into a separate candidate.

summary: This snapshot is Netty master (5.0.0.Final-SNAPSHOT) and contains only main sources (1,851 files, no tests, no binaries skipped). The strongest source-supported issue is in the HTTP/1 codec: the decoder chooses body framing from Transfer-Encoding: chunked without rejecting or stripping a coexisting Content-Length, and Content-Length itself is only read as a single un-normalized value. That creates the classic request-smuggling ambiguity (CWE-444 / CWE-436), and the encoder path preserves both conflicting headers when a message is forwarded. I selected this single candidate; multiple plausible-but-later-timeline leads (Zlib/Bzip2 allocation, multipart temp files, SniHandler, HttpPostRequestDecoder DoS, XML DTD behavior) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed.
